record.paper_title: Open problems in Euclidean Ramsey Theory
record.original_question: Frankl and Rödl define a finite set A to be super-Ramsey if, for sufficiently large N, there are subsets X of E^N of size less than c^N such that every subset Y of X with no copy of A has size less than |X|/(1+ε)^N, for some positive constants c and ε. Are the super-Ramsey finite sets exactly the spherical finite sets?

evidence.quote: Frankl and Rödl define the following stronger concept
the super-Ramsey sets are just the spherical sets

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Work in Euclidean space $E^N = \mathbb{R}^N$ with the standard Euclidean metric. A copy of a finite set $A \subset E^k$ in $E^N$ is the image of $A$ under an isometric embedding $E^k \hookrightarrow E^N$. A finite set $A \subset \mathbb{R}^k$ is called spherical if it is contained in some Euclidean sphere (equivalently, the affine span of $A$ contains a point equidistant from all points of $A$).

Call a finite set $A$ super-Ramsey if there exist constants $c > 1$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $N$, there is a subset $X \subseteq E^N$ with $|X| < c^N$ such that every $Y \subseteq X$ which contains no congruent copy of $A$ satisfies 
$$|Y| < \frac{|X|}{(1+\varepsilon)^N}.$$

Question: Is it true that the super-Ramsey finite sets are exactly the spherical finite sets?
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and papers (2024–2025) on Euclidean Ramsey theory still discuss the conjecture that Ramsey sets coincide with spherical sets, and the stronger super-Ramsey property has been verified only for specific classes (rectangular sets, simplices, certain transitive sets). No source indicates the full characterization "super-Ramsey = spherical" has been established; it remains an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Nearly all known Euclidean Ramsey sets are subsoluble
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses status of Ramsey vs spherical sets; super-Ramsey known only for restricted classes.
status_evidence.claim: Characterization of super-Ramsey sets remains open.

status_evidence.title: Non-spherical sets versus lines in Euclidean Ramsey theory
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work targets the Ramsey=spherical conjecture; the stronger super-Ramsey version is not resolved.

status_evidence.title: Euclidean Ramsey Theory (Graham)
status_evidence.snippet: Frankl–Rödl proved rectangular sets are super-Ramsey; general characterization conjectural.
status_evidence.claim: Only partial results toward super-Ramsey = spherical.
